title: Kirpa Ram of Kashmir
hookLine: the pandit who led the plea to Guru Tegh Bahadur later joined the Khalsa and died at Chamkaur

cards: A parent's years. A stranger who pulled you out of the water. A teacher who saw something in you nobody else did.
None of those comes with a bill you can settle. What you can do is spend your life near the person, or the cause, that saved you. That's the shape of today's story.
It begins with a group of frightened men walking a long way from the mountains of Kashmir to Anandpur, to ask a Guru for help.

teach.b: Kirpa Ram was a pandit, a Hindu Brahmin scholar, from Kashmir. Tradition says that in his time the Kashmiri pandits were being pressed by the authorities to give up their faith, and they didn't know where to turn.

So Kirpa Ram led a group of them to Anandpur, to Guru Tegh Bahadur, and laid their plea before him. Tradition says the Guru sat in silence, troubled, and said that a holy person would have to offer his life to stop this.

teach.h: HE TAUGHT THE YOUNG GOBIND RAI.
teach.b: His young son, Gobind Rai, the future Guru Gobind Singh, asked who could be worthier than his father.
And Guru Tegh Bahadur, the story goes, told the pandits to send word: if the Guru can be made to change his faith, we will change ours too. He went to Delhi, and there he was executed.
Sikhs remember him as one who gave his life for the freedom of others to keep a faith that wasn't his own. Then the story turns back to Kirpa Ram. He didn't just go home.
Tradition says he stayed close to the Guru's house and taught the young Gobind Rai Sanskrit and the old texts.

Years later, when Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, Kirpa Ram took amrit and became Kirpa Singh. And tradition says he was among those who fell at Chamkaur, in the same battle as the Guru's elder sons.
The man who came to ask for help came back, and stayed, and served, all the way to Chamkaur. He didn't pay the debt off. He lived inside it.

how: Sikhs remember the Kashmiri pandits' plea to Guru Tegh Bahadur each year on the Guru's martyrdom day, and Kirpa Ram's later life as Kirpa Singh is told as part of the story of Chamkaur.

practice: Bring to mind one person, or one community, that helped you when you couldn't help yourself; let it be specific, where you were, what they did.

Notice the urge to settle the account and move on, and ask instead what staying near it would look like: a visit, a regular call, time given to the cause. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Kirpa Ram. The pandit who brought the plea to Guru Tegh Bahadur and, tradition says, came back to serve, became Kirpa Singh, and fell at Chamkaur.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirpa, grace; a word Sikhs use for God's grace, and the first part of Kirpa Ram's name.

carryVoice: Your line: he came back to serve. Not paid off, but lived in. Until tomorrow.
